attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post. He cites the Apple paper as backing, but the assertion is his.

semantics.note: Faithful to his categorical assertion of absence. The separate claim about agents is rightly left out.

contract.note: He named no measure. Reading 'reason' as verified multistep problem-solving is ordinary, and the contract avoids claims about inner mechanisms. It also fairly says that failure above a difficulty threshold does not prove total absence. The result still depends on this reading.

evidence.note: This is the Apple paper he cites, June 2025, primary source. Its simulator-checked puzzles show reasoning models solving multistep instances and beating non-thinking models at medium complexity, before collapsing beyond a threshold.

reviews.rationale: The contract scores a categorical claim that reasoning models lack multistep inference. The paper he cites shows verified multistep successes on puzzle instances of varied complexity, with a clear advantage at intermediate levels. Collapse at high complexity shows limits, not total absence. Under the fair behavioral reading, this meets the contradiction condition.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps the popup claim, the bloat claim, and the 'most of them hate' scope.

contract.note: Reading 'most' as a majority and 'hate' as strong dislike is ordinary. Treating 'bloat' and 'odd' as subjective is fair. June 2025 is a reasonable period to test.

evidence.note: Office Watch, Feb 2025. Documents Copilot prompts in Word and icons in Excel, but predates June and measures no user sentiment.
Office Watch, June 2025. Some plans have per-app off switches and others do not. Says nothing on majority sentiment.
UK government trial, late 2024. Positive sentiment, but from a restricted licensed population, not representative Word and Excel users in June 2025.

reviews.rationale: Interface reporting makes the popup complaint plausible but does not show how widespread prompts were in June 2025. No representative survey shows that most Word and Excel users strongly dislike Copilot. The UK trial's positive results cover a different population and period. The packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words. The context identifies OpenAI as the subject.

semantics.note: An unhedged 'will die', conditional on a funding shortfall. The antecedent is kept.

contract.note: Using the bottom of his range ($20bn) and completed twelve-month periods is reasonable. He gave no failure lag or definition of death.

evidence.note: SoftBank's own disclosure: $22.5bn invested in OpenAI on Dec 26, 2025. That falls inside every qualifying twelve-month period, so it bears on the antecedent, not the predicted outcome.

reviews.rationale: This is a conditional forecast. The antecedent, OpenAI receiving less than $20bn in a year, did not occur in any completed period checked, because SoftBank alone invested $22.5bn in Dec 2025. With the condition unmet, the forecast cannot be scored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: A claim about what OpenAI's plan was at the time. The drafter correctly treats it as an observation of a planning state.

contract.note: Reading 'lose' as cumulative net losses is ordinary, and the contract flags the cash-burn ambiguity. Using June 2025 for the planning state is reasonable.

evidence.note: Oct 2024 report of a projected $44bn in losses for 2023-28. That is an earlier plan, not the one in force in June 2025.
Sept 2025 Reuters report of a $115bn cash-burn projection through 2029. It is a later plan and a different metric (cash burn, not net losses).

reviews.rationale: Neither item shows the net-loss projection in force in June 2025. One is from an earlier plan, the other from a later plan using a different metric. The underlying documents were not available. The packet does not settle whether the June 2025 plan projected over $100bn in net losses before profitability.
